Title: Extracting Soil Moisture Spectral Patterns Using Hyperspectral Imagery (HyspIm)

Overview and hyperspectral signatures of soil moisture
- Hyperspectral imaging exposes continuous absorption features that couple moisture to strong reflectance changes in the visible–NIR and shortwave infrared (SWIR), enabling pattern-based retrieval of near-surface soil moisture at scale. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">The advent of hyperspectral imagery allows examination of continuous spectra where contiguous narrow bands reveal characteristics of related absorption features and their interactions, providing sensitivity to moisture effects beyond isolated multispectral bands.
- Moisture primarily alters reflectance in SWIR water absorption bands near 1450–1950 nm and in the red-edge/NIR transitions, with additional sensitivity in the blue/green due to mineralogical and organic effects. <cite id="9047610c-1">Models for surface soil moisture using hyperspectral reflectance achieved R2 > 0.933 when built from selected bands around 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm, highlighting strong moisture sensitivity in the SWIR water absorption regions.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-4">Laboratory analyses across 28 European soils show organic carbon and texture control how moisture changes shortwave infrared reflectance, implying that soil property–moisture interactions modulate SWIR moisture signatures.</cite>
- Angle-based indices exploit directional sensitivity to surface water content, and hyperspectral band grouping improves moisture discrimination. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">A new hyperspectral spectral angle index using spectral regions 350–2500 nm and in‑situ ASD spectra achieved R2 = 0.9432 with soil percent moisture, while related indices such as Perpendicular Drought Index (PDI, R2 = 0.9537) and Normalized Multi-band Drought Index (NMDI, R2 = 0.9335) also showed high performance.</cite>

Preprocessing and materials handling for bare-soil moisture mapping
- Soil spectral libraries and resampling to sensor sampling functions are essential to represent diverse soils and reduce redundancy; spectral angle mapper (SAM) screening can reduce candidate soil spectra prior to modeling. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">A global soil spectral library with tens of thousands of 1 nm spectra was resampled to match Sentinel-2 sampling using cubic spline weights and incorporated into PROSAIL inversions; SAM was used to classify similar soil spectra and remove redundancy before inversion.</cite>
- Moisture introduces strong spectral perturbations across 400–2400 nm, affecting reflectance in mineral and organic bands; class-aware preprocessing or synthetic drying improves downstream predictions. <cite id="f28e28d3-2">Soil moisture hampers estimation of clay by reducing strength of absorption features; when models are stratified by moisture level or synthetically dry spectra are generated from wet spectra, accuracy improves, demonstrating that moisture strongly modulates the entire 400–2400 nm spectrum and must be handled explicitly.</cite>
- Practical preprocessing includes noise reduction and band compression, with evidence that key moisture indices can be preserved after reconstruction if informative bands are retained. <cite id="85a2c43b-3">Even after significant spectral compression and hyperspectral data reconstruction, NDMI retains moisture contrasts; high NDMI areas correspond to vegetation/water while red hues indicate dry soil, validating that essential moisture indices can be derived post-compression when spectral fidelity of key bands is preserved.</cite>

Feature extraction: moisture indices and spectral pattern mining
- Classical and hyperspectral variants of moisture indices leverage NIR–SWIR contrasts and can be tuned to soil-dominated pixels. <cite id="85a2c43b-1">NDMI computed from NIR and SWIR increases with surface moisture and is widely used to estimate soil surface moisture from spaceborne sensors.</cite> <cite id="85a2c43b-4">Evidence across studies shows NDMI correlates moderately to strongly with gravimetric soil moisture and can be used to screen soil moisture in sparse vegetation, with linear regressions yielding average errors below 5% and high linearity in certain contexts.</cite>
- Hyperspectral angle indices and multi-band formulations exploit soil-specific spectral geometry and band groupings to enhance sensitivity. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">PDI and NMDI tied to specific spectral regions showed high R2 with soil moisture, and a new angle index designed for 350–2500 nm achieved R2 = 0.9432; MODIS-relevant band groupings also maintained R2 ≈ 0.72, illustrating portability and the value of contiguous bands.</cite>
- Wavelength selection around SWIR water bands and red-edge improves predictive performance and interpretability. <cite id="9047610c-1">Selecting reflectance around 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm produced accurate soil moisture models (R2 > 0.933) across multiple textures, aligning with known water absorption features that deepen/shallow as moisture increases.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">Chemometric and hyperspectral studies demonstrate that informative wavelengths can be identified and selected to build robust soil moisture models, addressing spectral redundancy and noise inherent in hyperspectral data.</cite>

Modeling strategies: empirical, machine learning, and physics-based
- Empirical band-ratio and angle-index models provide rapid mapping with strong in‑situ performance when calibrated on bare soil spectra. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">PDI, NMDI, and a new hyperspectral angle index achieved R2 up to 0.9537, indicating that simple ratios and spectral geometry can capture moisture patterns in soil spectra.</cite>
- Chemometric learners (e.g., PLSR) and spectral selection are effective on hyperspectral cubes and hyperspectral video, especially when combined with segmentation of bare-soil regions. <cite id="9047610c-2">Partial least squares applied to Hyperion imagery and region-based segmentation successfully quantified soil moisture relationships, selected informative wavelengths, and improved prediction accuracy and robustness by reducing spectral redundancy.</cite>
- Physics-based radiative transfer models offer interpretability and transferability across moisture regimes by representing soil and canopy layers. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL integrates PROSPECT leaf optics with SAIL canopy geometry and soil reflectance to simulate canopy reflectance; soil reflectances from a global library can be used to constrain inversions, and SAM-based classification reduces redundancy in soil spectra used for modeling.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-4">PROSAIL has been assessed for suitability with future hyperspectral environments in agriculture, highlighting its potential for modeling soil–canopy interactions under high spectral resolution.</cite>
- Semi-empirical albedo modeling provides a bridge between moisture–reflectance physics and data-driven calibration using broad spectral coverage. <cite id="9047610c-3">The General Spectral Vector (GSV) soil albedo model represents hyperspectral soil reflectance as a linear combination of dry and wet spectral vectors derived from 23,871 soil spectra, enabling moisture-dependent albedo simulation across wavelengths for soil moisture retrievals.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-4">Moisture dependence of soil reflectance varies with organic carbon and texture, supporting semi-empirical models that couple soil properties with moisture to improve reflectance estimates.</cite>

Validation, performance, and controlling variables
- Performance depends on soil texture, mineralogy, and salinity; stratifying by texture or moisture class improves accuracy. <cite id="9047610c-1">Across three textures, moisture models built on 1460/1900/2010 nm achieved R2 > 0.933; when textures were mixed, soil moisture remained accurately retrieved (R2 = 0.937), though salt content models degraded without stratification and improved to R2 = 0.951 after moisture-stratified calibration.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">Moisture–salt effects are strong; hyperspectral studies emphasize that non-salted soil results may not transfer to saline settings, motivating salinity-aware spectral modeling in arid regions.</cite>
- Vegetation cover and salinity confound soil moisture signals; best results occur when vegetation is minimal or masked, and indices are tuned to soil. <cite id="85a2c43b-4">Evidence supports NDMI screening for soil moisture in zones with poor vegetation cover, with linear regressions yielding small errors; in contrast, studies in non-irrigated conditions show NDMI correlates moderately and is best used for bare soil or low-vegetation periods.</cite>
- Moisture induces broad spectral shifts that interact with soil properties; models that account for these interactions are more robust. <cite id="9047610c-4">Organic carbon and texture control moisture dependence of soil reflectance in the SWIR, implying that soil property priors should inform feature selection and model calibration to disambiguate moisture from mineral/organic effects.</cite>

Operational considerations: airborne vs. satellite HyspIm and scale
- Airborne hyperspectral imagers (e.g., Hyperion/PRISMA-class) capture contiguous narrow bands that resolve moisture features but require careful preprocessing and atmospheric/illumination treatment; satellite HyspIm trades resolution for coverage. <cite id="9047610c-2">Hyperspectral imaging onboard or satellite-borne platforms provides high spectral redundancy; preprocessing and informative wavelength selection are necessary to reduce noise and redundancy before inversion for soil moisture.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-0">Soil reflectance libraries and resampling to sensor spectral response functions are needed to align simulated and measured spectra; SAM-based classification reduces redundancy before inversion.</cite>
- Moisture effects span broad spectral regions; band-reduction and reconstruction approaches must preserve SWIR moisture bands to retain performance. <cite id="85a2c43b-3">NDMI computed from reconstructed compressed hyperspectral data retained moisture contrasts, with high NDMI associated with vegetation/water and red tones indicating dry soil, validating the feasibility of band-efficient HyspIm workflows when moisture-sensitive bands are preserved.</cite>

A practical workflow for extracting soil moisture spectral patterns (HyspIm)
1) Material identification and masking
- Segment scene into bare soil, vegetation, and water; prioritize bare-soil pixels for moisture mapping, or unmix to estimate soil proportion and apply subpixel corrections. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">Indices designed for soil moisture (PDI, NMDI, spectral angle index) were developed on in‑situ soil spectra and show high R2, underscoring the importance of soil-targeted material handling.</cite>
- Use a global soil spectral library and SAM to classify and reduce redundant soil endmembers for modeling. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">SAM-assigned soil classes from a global 1‑nm library, resampled to sensor response, were used to constrain PROSAIL inversions and reduce redundancy.</cite>

2) Preprocessing
- Apply dark-object subtraction and smoothing (SG or derivative, as appropriate) to reduce noise; correct illumination and atmospheric effects. <cite id="9047610c-2">Hyperspectral preprocessing and informative wavelength selection are necessary to eliminate redundant variables and reduce noise prior to modeling.</cite>
- Where needed, stratify by moisture class or generate synthetically dry spectra from wet measurements to mitigate moisture-induced spectral overlap. <cite id="f28e28d3-2">Stratifying by moisture level or synthetically drying wet spectra improved clay estimation accuracy, demonstrating that moisture-driven spectral changes must be explicitly addressed to avoid bias.</cite>

3) Feature extraction
- Compute moisture indices emphasizing NIR–SWIR contrasts: NDMI (NIR–SWIR normalized), MSI (SWIR/NIR), and hyperspectral angle indices; select informative wavelengths around 1460–1900 nm and red-edge. <cite id="85a2c43b-1">NDMI computed from NIR and SWIR increases with moisture and is suitable for soil surface moisture mapping.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-1">PDI, NMDI, and a new hyperspectral angle index tied to 350–2500 nm achieved high R2 with soil moisture.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Bands near 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm drive strong soil moisture relationships.</cite>

4) Modeling
- Empirical/chemometric models: PLSR/SVM on selected bands; evaluate sensitivity to soil texture and salinity, and stratify by moisture class. <cite id="9047610c-2">PLSR on hyperspectral segments selected for informative wavelengths yielded accurate and robust soil moisture predictions.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Texture and salinity co-vary with moisture signals; stratification by moisture class improved salt-related model performance, illustrating the need for domain-aware calibration.</cite>
- Physics-based models: Use PROSAIL or Soil-PROSPECT-like formulations with soil reflectance from spectral libraries; incorporate moisture dependence through wet/dry vectors or parameter priors. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL integrates soil reflectance and canopy geometry, leveraging global soil spectra and SAM classification to constrain inversions.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-3">GSV soil albedo represents hyperspectral reflectance as a combination of dry and wet spectral vectors derived from large soil spectral datasets, enabling moisture-aware reflectance simulation in models.</cite>

5) Validation and cross-sensor checks
- Validate with gravimetric moisture; compare indices across sensors (MODIS/ASTER/ALI/ETM+) and assess portability of band groupings. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">In‑situ calibration showed high correlations for PDI and NMDI, and MODIS-relevant band groupings retained R2 ≈ 0.72, supporting cross-sensor portability of hyperspectral moisture indices.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Soil moisture models built on 1460/1900/2010 nm achieved R2 > 0.933, aligning with known water band positions and offering transferable features for cross-sensor validation.</cite>

Key challenges and limitations
- Spectral variability from soil properties and surface roughness: moisture effects interact with organic matter, texture, and color, requiring soil-specific calibrations and semi-empirical corrections. <cite id="9047610c-4">Organic carbon and texture control moisture dependence of soil reflectance, necessitating models that incorporate soil properties to disambiguate moisture from mineral/organic signals.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-3">Soil albedo depends on intrinsic characteristics and volumetric water content; coupling dry and wet spectral vectors improves moisture-aware reflectance modeling.</cite>
- Vegetation coupling: indices that work well on bare soil degrade under dense canopies; use low-vegetation periods, spectral masking, or PROSAIL-based canopy disentangling. <cite id="85a2c43b-4">NDMI is appropriate for screening soil moisture in sparse vegetation; in irrigated and non-irrigated conditions, best results occur for bare soil or low-vegetation cover.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL’s representation of soil reflectance beneath canopy canopies helps separate vegetation from soil moisture signals under hyperspectral resolution.</cite>
- Data volume and redundancy: leverage SAM, SNV/MSC, and continuum analysis to manage hyperspectral redundancy and improve model stability. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">SAM classification reduced redundancy among soil reflectances prior to inversion in PROSAIL-based workflows.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">Preprocessing and informative wavelength selection are necessary to reduce noise and redundancy in hyperspectral data for robust moisture modeling.</cite>

Summary of actionable spectral patterns for HyspIm
- Target moisture-sensitive SWIR bands (≈1460–1900 nm) and red-edge/NIR transitions for band selection or index design; incorporate angle-based sensitivity where surface orientation is controllable. <cite id="9047610c-1">Models using bands near 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm achieved R2 > 0.933, demonstrating strong moisture sensitivity in SWIR water absorption features.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-1">Angle indices PDI and NMDI and a hyperspectral angle index tied to 350–2500 nm achieved up to R2 = 0.9537–0.9432, showing the value of spectral geometry and contiguous band grouping.</cite>
- When using physical models, couple soil reflectance libraries with moisture-dependent albedo vectors and canopy treatment; when using empirical models, stratify by soil type and moisture class and validate with gravimetric data. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL with global soil spectral libraries and SAM-based soil endmember reduction supports moisture-aware inversion.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-3">GSV soil albedo models moisture dependence through dry/wet spectral vectors over 400–2500 nm for hyperspectral mapping.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Texture and salinity modulate moisture–reflectance relationships; stratification and targeted wavelength selection improve accuracy.</cite>

Practical guidance
- Start with SAM-based bare-soil segmentation and compute NDMI/MSI across red-edge/SWIR bands; select features around 1460–1900 nm and evaluate angle indices; build PLSR/SVM models with moisture-class stratification and validate against gravimetric samples. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">High-performing soil moisture indices (PDI, NMDI, new angle index) calibrated on in‑situ soil spectra provide a rapid baseline for mapping.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">PLSR with region-based segmentation and wavelength selection improves robustness and accuracy in hyperspectral soil moisture mapping.</cite>
- For broader coverage or mountainous terrain, adopt PROSAIL inversion with soil spectral vectors and moisture-dependent albedo to account for canopy and soil moisture coupling; use cross-sensor checks to ensure portability of indices. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL integrates soil and canopy reflectance with global soil spectral libraries and SAM classification to constrain inversions under hyperspectral resolution.</cite> <cite id="85a2c43b-1">NDMI’s NIR–SWIR formulation remains interpretable and portable across sensors for soil surface moisture screening.</cite>

The purpose of this study was to develop a hyperspectral imaging technique to predict soil moisture content. Title: Extracting Soil Moisture Spectral Patterns Using Hyperspectral Imagery (HyspIm)

Overview and hyperspectral signatures of soil moisture
- Hyperspectral imaging exposes continuous absorption features that couple moisture to strong reflectance changes in the visible–NIR and shortwave infrared (SWIR), enabling pattern-based retrieval of near-surface soil moisture at scale. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">The advent of hyperspectral imagery allows examination of continuous spectra where contiguous narrow bands reveal characteristics of related absorption features and their interactions, providing sensitivity to moisture effects beyond isolated multispectral bands.
- Moisture primarily alters reflectance in SWIR water absorption bands near 1450–1950 nm and in the red-edge/NIR transitions, with additional sensitivity in the blue/green due to mineralogical and organic effects. <cite id="9047610c-1">Models for surface soil moisture using hyperspectral reflectance achieved R2 > 0.933 when built from selected bands around 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm, highlighting strong moisture sensitivity in the SWIR water absorption regions.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-4">Laboratory analyses across 28 European soils show organic carbon and texture control how moisture changes shortwave infrared reflectance, implying that soil property–moisture interactions modulate SWIR moisture signatures.</cite>
- Angle-based indices exploit directional sensitivity to surface water content, and hyperspectral band grouping improves moisture discrimination. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">A new hyperspectral spectral angle index using spectral regions 350–2500 nm and in‑situ ASD spectra achieved R2 = 0.9432 with soil percent moisture, while related indices such as Perpendicular Drought Index (PDI, R2 = 0.9537) and Normalized Multi-band Drought Index (NMDI, R2 = 0.9335) also showed high performance.</cite>

Preprocessing and materials handling for bare-soil moisture mapping
- Soil spectral libraries and resampling to sensor sampling functions are essential to represent diverse soils and reduce redundancy; spectral angle mapper (SAM) screening can reduce candidate soil spectra prior to modeling. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">A global soil spectral library with tens of thousands of 1 nm spectra was resampled to match Sentinel-2 sampling using cubic spline weights and incorporated into PROSAIL inversions; SAM was used to classify similar soil spectra and remove redundancy before inversion.</cite>
- Moisture introduces strong spectral perturbations across 400–2400 nm, affecting reflectance in mineral and organic bands; class-aware preprocessing or synthetic drying improves downstream predictions. <cite id="f28e28d3-2">Soil moisture hampers estimation of clay by reducing strength of absorption features; when models are stratified by moisture level or synthetically dry spectra are generated from wet spectra, accuracy improves, demonstrating that moisture strongly modulates the entire 400–2400 nm spectrum and must be handled explicitly.</cite>
- Practical preprocessing includes noise reduction and band compression, with evidence that key moisture indices can be preserved after reconstruction if informative bands are retained. <cite id="85a2c43b-3">Even after significant spectral compression and hyperspectral data reconstruction, NDMI retains moisture contrasts; high NDMI areas correspond to vegetation/water while red hues indicate dry soil, validating that essential moisture indices can be derived post-compression when spectral fidelity of key bands is preserved.</cite>

Feature extraction: moisture indices and spectral pattern mining
- Classical and hyperspectral variants of moisture indices leverage NIR–SWIR contrasts and can be tuned to soil-dominated pixels. <cite id="85a2c43b-1">NDMI computed from NIR and SWIR increases with surface moisture and is widely used to estimate soil surface moisture from spaceborne sensors.</cite> <cite id="85a2c43b-4">Evidence across studies shows NDMI correlates moderately to strongly with gravimetric soil moisture and can be used to screen soil moisture in sparse vegetation, with linear regressions yielding average errors below 5% and high linearity in certain contexts.</cite>
- Hyperspectral angle indices and multi-band formulations exploit soil-specific spectral geometry and band groupings to enhance sensitivity. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">PDI and NMDI tied to specific spectral regions showed high R2 with soil moisture, and a new angle index designed for 350–2500 nm achieved R2 = 0.9432; MODIS-relevant band groupings also maintained R2 ≈ 0.72, illustrating portability and the value of contiguous bands.</cite>
- Wavelength selection around SWIR water bands and red-edge improves predictive performance and interpretability. <cite id="9047610c-1">Selecting reflectance around 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm produced accurate soil moisture models (R2 > 0.933) across multiple textures, aligning with known water absorption features that deepen/shallow as moisture increases.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">Chemometric and hyperspectral studies demonstrate that informative wavelengths can be identified and selected to build robust soil moisture models, addressing spectral redundancy and noise inherent in hyperspectral data.</cite>

Modeling strategies: empirical, machine learning, and physics-based
- Empirical band-ratio and angle-index models provide rapid mapping with strong in‑situ performance when calibrated on bare soil spectra. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">PDI, NMDI, and a new hyperspectral angle index achieved R2 up to 0.9537, indicating that simple ratios and spectral geometry can capture moisture patterns in soil spectra.</cite>
- Chemometric learners (e.g., PLSR) and spectral selection are effective on hyperspectral cubes and hyperspectral video, especially when combined with segmentation of bare-soil regions. <cite id="9047610c-2">Partial least squares applied to Hyperion imagery and region-based segmentation successfully quantified soil moisture relationships, selected informative wavelengths, and improved prediction accuracy and robustness by reducing spectral redundancy.</cite>
- Physics-based radiative transfer models offer interpretability and transferability across moisture regimes by representing soil and canopy layers. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL integrates PROSPECT leaf optics with SAIL canopy geometry and soil reflectance to simulate canopy reflectance; soil reflectances from a global library can be used to constrain inversions, and SAM-based classification reduces redundancy in soil spectra used for modeling.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-4">PROSAIL has been assessed for suitability with future hyperspectral environments in agriculture, highlighting its potential for modeling soil–canopy interactions under high spectral resolution.</cite>
- Semi-empirical albedo modeling provides a bridge between moisture–reflectance physics and data-driven calibration using broad spectral coverage. <cite id="9047610c-3">The General Spectral Vector (GSV) soil albedo model represents hyperspectral soil reflectance as a linear combination of dry and wet spectral vectors derived from 23,871 soil spectra, enabling moisture-dependent albedo simulation across wavelengths for soil moisture retrievals.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-4">Moisture dependence of soil reflectance varies with organic carbon and texture, supporting semi-empirical models that couple soil properties with moisture to improve reflectance estimates.</cite>

Validation, performance, and controlling variables
- Performance depends on soil texture, mineralogy, and salinity; stratifying by texture or moisture class improves accuracy. <cite id="9047610c-1">Across three textures, moisture models built on 1460/1900/2010 nm achieved R2 > 0.933; when textures were mixed, soil moisture remained accurately retrieved (R2 = 0.937), though salt content models degraded without stratification and improved to R2 = 0.951 after moisture-stratified calibration.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">Moisture–salt effects are strong; hyperspectral studies emphasize that non-salted soil results may not transfer to saline settings, motivating salinity-aware spectral modeling in arid regions.</cite>
- Vegetation cover and salinity confound soil moisture signals; best results occur when vegetation is minimal or masked, and indices are tuned to soil. <cite id="85a2c43b-4">Evidence supports NDMI screening for soil moisture in zones with poor vegetation cover, with linear regressions yielding small errors; in contrast, studies in non-irrigated conditions show NDMI correlates moderately and is best used for bare soil or low-vegetation periods.</cite>
- Moisture induces broad spectral shifts that interact with soil properties; models that account for these interactions are more robust. <cite id="9047610c-4">Organic carbon and texture control moisture dependence of soil reflectance in the SWIR, implying that soil property priors should inform feature selection and model calibration to disambiguate moisture from mineral/organic effects.</cite>

Operational considerations: airborne vs. satellite HyspIm and scale
- Airborne hyperspectral imagers (e.g., Hyperion/PRISMA-class) capture contiguous narrow bands that resolve moisture features but require careful preprocessing and atmospheric/illumination treatment; satellite HyspIm trades resolution for coverage. <cite id="9047610c-2">Hyperspectral imaging onboard or satellite-borne platforms provides high spectral redundancy; preprocessing and informative wavelength selection are necessary to reduce noise and redundancy before inversion for soil moisture.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-0">Soil reflectance libraries and resampling to sensor spectral response functions are needed to align simulated and measured spectra; SAM-based classification reduces redundancy before inversion.</cite>
- Moisture effects span broad spectral regions; band-reduction and reconstruction approaches must preserve SWIR moisture bands to retain performance. <cite id="85a2c43b-3">NDMI computed from reconstructed compressed hyperspectral data retained moisture contrasts, with high NDMI associated with vegetation/water and red tones indicating dry soil, validating the feasibility of band-efficient HyspIm workflows when moisture-sensitive bands are preserved.</cite>

A practical workflow for extracting soil moisture spectral patterns (HyspIm)
1) Material identification and masking
- Segment scene into bare soil, vegetation, and water; prioritize bare-soil pixels for moisture mapping, or unmix to estimate soil proportion and apply subpixel corrections. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">Indices designed for soil moisture (PDI, NMDI, spectral angle index) were developed on in‑situ soil spectra and show high R2, underscoring the importance of soil-targeted material handling.</cite>
- Use a global soil spectral library and SAM to classify and reduce redundant soil endmembers for modeling. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">SAM-assigned soil classes from a global 1‑nm library, resampled to sensor response, were used to constrain PROSAIL inversions and reduce redundancy.</cite>

2) Preprocessing
- Apply dark-object subtraction and smoothing (SG or derivative, as appropriate) to reduce noise; correct illumination and atmospheric effects. <cite id="9047610c-2">Hyperspectral preprocessing and informative wavelength selection are necessary to eliminate redundant variables and reduce noise prior to modeling.</cite>
- Where needed, stratify by moisture class or generate synthetically dry spectra from wet measurements to mitigate moisture-induced spectral overlap. <cite id="f28e28d3-2">Stratifying by moisture level or synthetically drying wet spectra improved clay estimation accuracy, demonstrating that moisture-driven spectral changes must be explicitly addressed to avoid bias.</cite>

3) Feature extraction
- Compute moisture indices emphasizing NIR–SWIR contrasts: NDMI (NIR–SWIR normalized), MSI (SWIR/NIR), and hyperspectral angle indices; select informative wavelengths around 1460–1900 nm and red-edge. <cite id="85a2c43b-1">NDMI computed from NIR and SWIR increases with moisture and is suitable for soil surface moisture mapping.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-1">PDI, NMDI, and a new hyperspectral angle index tied to 350–2500 nm achieved high R2 with soil moisture.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Bands near 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm drive strong soil moisture relationships.</cite>

4) Modeling
- Empirical/chemometric models: PLSR/SVM on selected bands; evaluate sensitivity to soil texture and salinity, and stratify by moisture class. <cite id="9047610c-2">PLSR on hyperspectral segments selected for informative wavelengths yielded accurate and robust soil moisture predictions.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Texture and salinity co-vary with moisture signals; stratification by moisture class improved salt-related model performance, illustrating the need for domain-aware calibration.</cite>
- Physics-based models: Use PROSAIL or Soil-PROSPECT-like formulations with soil reflectance from spectral libraries; incorporate moisture dependence through wet/dry vectors or parameter priors. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL integrates soil reflectance and canopy geometry, leveraging global soil spectra and SAM classification to constrain inversions.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-3">GSV soil albedo represents hyperspectral reflectance as a combination of dry and wet spectral vectors derived from large soil spectral datasets, enabling moisture-aware reflectance simulation in models.</cite>

5) Validation and cross-sensor checks
- Validate with gravimetric moisture; compare indices across sensors (MODIS/ASTER/ALI/ETM+) and assess portability of band groupings. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">In‑situ calibration showed high correlations for PDI and NMDI, and MODIS-relevant band groupings retained R2 ≈ 0.72, supporting cross-sensor portability of hyperspectral moisture indices.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Soil moisture models built on 1460/1900/2010 nm achieved R2 > 0.933, aligning with known water band positions and offering transferable features for cross-sensor validation.</cite>

Key challenges and limitations
- Spectral variability from soil properties and surface roughness: moisture effects interact with organic matter, texture, and color, requiring soil-specific calibrations and semi-empirical corrections. <cite id="9047610c-4">Organic carbon and texture control moisture dependence of soil reflectance, necessitating models that incorporate soil properties to disambiguate moisture from mineral/organic signals.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-3">Soil albedo depends on intrinsic characteristics and volumetric water content; coupling dry and wet spectral vectors improves moisture-aware reflectance modeling.</cite>
- Vegetation coupling: indices that work well on bare soil degrade under dense canopies; use low-vegetation periods, spectral masking, or PROSAIL-based canopy disentangling. <cite id="85a2c43b-4">NDMI is appropriate for screening soil moisture in sparse vegetation; in irrigated and non-irrigated conditions, best results occur for bare soil or low-vegetation cover.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL’s representation of soil reflectance beneath canopy canopies helps separate vegetation from soil moisture signals under hyperspectral resolution.</cite>
- Data volume and redundancy: leverage SAM, SNV/MSC, and continuum analysis to manage hyperspectral redundancy and improve model stability. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">SAM classification reduced redundancy among soil reflectances prior to inversion in PROSAIL-based workflows.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">Preprocessing and informative wavelength selection are necessary to reduce noise and redundancy in hyperspectral data for robust moisture modeling.</cite>

Summary of actionable spectral patterns for HyspIm
- Target moisture-sensitive SWIR bands (≈1460–1900 nm) and red-edge/NIR transitions for band selection or index design; incorporate angle-based sensitivity where surface orientation is controllable. <cite id="9047610c-1">Models using bands near 1460, 1900, and 2010 nm achieved R2 > 0.933, demonstrating strong moisture sensitivity in SWIR water absorption features.</cite> <cite id="f28e28d3-1">Angle indices PDI and NMDI and a hyperspectral angle index tied to 350–2500 nm achieved up to R2 = 0.9537–0.9432, showing the value of spectral geometry and contiguous band grouping.</cite>
- When using physical models, couple soil reflectance libraries with moisture-dependent albedo vectors and canopy treatment; when using empirical models, stratify by soil type and moisture class and validate with gravimetric data. <cite id="f28e28d3-0">PROSAIL with global soil spectral libraries and SAM-based soil endmember reduction supports moisture-aware inversion.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-3">GSV soil albedo models moisture dependence through dry/wet spectral vectors over 400–2500 nm for hyperspectral mapping.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-1">Texture and salinity modulate moisture–reflectance relationships; stratification and targeted wavelength selection improve accuracy.</cite>

Practical guidance
- Start with SAM-based bare-soil segmentation and compute NDMI/MSI across red-edge/SWIR bands; select features around 1460–1900 nm and evaluate angle indices; build PLSR/SVM models with moisture-class stratification and validate against gravimetric samples. <cite id="f28e28d3-1">High-performing soil moisture indices (PDI, NMDI, new angle index) calibrated on in‑situ soil spectra provide a rapid baseline for mapping.</cite> <cite id="9047610c-2">PLSR with region-based segmentation and wavelength selection improves robustness and accuracy in hyperspectral soil moisture mapping.</cite>

Title: Reducing the Influence of Soil Moisture on the Estimation of Clay from Hyperspectral Data: A Case Study Using Simulated PRISMA Data
Snippet: Soil moisture hampers the estimation of soil variables such as clay content from remote and proximal sensing data, reducing the strength of the relevant spectral absorption features. In the present study, two different strategies have been evaluated for their ability to minimize the influence of soil moisture on clay estimation by using soil spectra acquired in a laboratory and by simulating satellite hyperspectral data. Simulated satellite data were obtained according to the spectral characteristics of the forthcoming hyperspectral imager on board of the Italian PRISMA satellite mission. The soil datasets were split into four groups according to the water content. For each soil moisture level a prediction model was applied, using either spectral indices or partial least squares regression (PLSR). Prediction models were either specifically developed for the soil moisture level or calibrated using synthetically dry soil spectra, generated from wet soil data. Synthetically dry spectra were obtained using a new technique based on the effects caused by soil moisture on the optical spectrum from 400 to 2400 nm. The estimation of soil clay content, when using different prediction models according to soil moisture, was slightly more accurate as compared to the use of synthetically dry soil spectra, both employing clay indices and PLSR models. The results obtained in this study demonstrate that the a priori knowledge of the soil moisture class can reduce the error of clay estimation when using hyperspectral remote sensing data, such as those that will be provided by the PRISMA satellite mission in the near future.

MSI is calculated as a ratio of the SWIR spectrum and near-infrared spectrum (NIR) and measures the degree of stress due to moisture deficiency. NDMI assists in estimating moisture content in plants and soil as a function of the difference in the variation of the NIR and SWIR wavelengths. The indices are also used extensively to analyze the condition of soils, as poor quality or eroded land loses its moisture-retaining capacity, resulting in desiccation and disintegration. In addition to albedo and vegetation index estimation, soil moisture analysis provides an overall idea of the soil's condition and its susceptibility to the erosion process. From individual approaches such as vegetation indices, albedo, and soil moisture, identification of universal indicators of erosion is feasible. However, combined methods must be used to perform an in-depth analysis of soil erosion. One of these methods is integrating albedo analysis and soil moisture evaluation. High albedo values and low moisture indices characterize degraded areas. Integrating these parameters enables more precise determination of the erodible regions, particularly in arid areas where wind erosion is dominant. Combining MSI and albedo analysis enables the detection of areas with high albedo reflection and low moisture content, indicating susceptibility to erosion and soil degradation. However, the issue of remote sensing screening of soil moisture content in desert and arid regions remains debatable, as Koohbanani & Yazdani (2018) provided the evidence that NDMI is an appropriate indicator to screen soil moisture content, especially in the zones with poor vegetation cover. The study, recently conducted in Indonesia, provided strong evidence to support the possibility of deriving soil moisture content from spatial NDMI values using a linear regression function with the average error of less than 5% and 94.6% linearity (Cahyono et al., 2022). Another scientific evidence in support of the possibility of estimating soil moisture content using NDMI values was provided by Kılıç & Gündoğan (2022), who found that NDMI had a moderately significant positive correlation with soil moisture content, identified by the gravimetric method. To obtain the best results, it is believed that NDMI screening should be performed for bare soil or during periods of low presence of vegetation cover.

Therefore, the combination of NDMI and EVI could be used to create maps for precision irrigation and nitrogen application in the systems of digital agriculture (Šuslikova et al., 2023).

Title: Prediction of Soil Moisture Content and Soil Salt Concentration from Hyperspectral Laboratory and Field Data
Snippet: This research examines the simultaneous retrieval of surface soil moisture and salt concentrations using hyperspectral reflectance data in an arid environment. We conducted laboratory and outdoor field experiments in which we examined three key soil variables: soil moisture, salt and texture (silty loam, clay and silty clay). The soil moisture content models for multiple textures (M_SMC models) were based on selected hyperspectral reflectance data located around 1460, 1900 and 2010 nm and resulted in R2 values higher than 0.933. Meanwhile, the soil salt concentrations were also accurately (R2 > 0.748) modeled (M_SSC models) based on wavebands located at 540, 1740, 2010 and 2350 nm. When the different texture samples were mixed (SL + C + SC models), soil moisture was still accurately retrieved (R2 = 0.937) but the soil salt not as well (R2 = 0.47). After stratifying the samples by retrieved soil moisture levels, the R2 of calibrated M_SSCSMC models for soil salt concentrations improved to 0.951. This two-step method also showed applicability for analyzing soil-salt samples in the field. The M_SSCSMC models resulted in R2 values equal to 0.912 when moisture is lower than 0.15, and R2 values equal to 0.481 when soil moisture is between 0.15 and 0.2.

Title: Nontradional Detection of Soil Moisture Content Based On Hyperspectral Imaging Technique
Snippet: Due to different inversion moisture content methods in soil, the inversion effect is also very different. 

A new spectral detection technology, named hyperspectral imaging technology, commonly used onboard or satellite borne imaging hyperspectral data sources (Galvao et al. 2008, Selige etal 2006, Gomez etal 2008). The partial least squares method was used to predict soil moisture content through Hyperion images, but results showed that the inversion accuracy of soil moisture content was very low (Zhang 2010). Hyperspectral imaging technology was used to invert the soil moisture content and adopt a variety of stoichiometric methods for analysis (Wei 2009). The relation between spectral reflectance and moisture content in soil surface was analyzed and achieved a good accuracy (Liu et al. 2004, Liu et al. 2011). The spectrum changes between moisture and salt in soil had a strong effect, and moisture content in soil was limited for different degrees of salinized soil (Liu et al. 2013). The studies above showed that the information extraction of soil moisture content based on hyperspectral imaging technology has practical feasibility, and achieves good results for relationship between different moisture content and spectrum of soil, which provide a method guidance and technical support for soil moisture monitoring. However, these methods are mostly as the research object of non-salted soil, and the effects of soil salinity on moisture and spectrum have not been considered to cause difficulty of application in arid areas. 

The purpose of this study was to develop a hyperspectral imaging technique to predict soil moisture content. Because a hyperspectral image provides both spatial and spectral information, it is constructed in a three-dimensional data format with very high spectral redundancy. Thus, preprocessing methods and informative wavelengths selection are typically necessary to eliminate redundant variables and reduce noise in hyperspectral images. The specific objectives of this study were to (1) acquire the soil spectral responses using a region-based segmentation technique from hyperspectral images, (2) build a quantitative model between spectral data and measured moisture values of soil using chemometrics techniques, (3) obtain the informative wavelengths, (4) develop a prediction model of soil moisture content with the wavelengths selected, (5) evaluate the performance of the prediction model built through robustness and accuracy.
